![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/e8cd8966d69260c77685d349c97eceb1545686d347f6cdb827ad470880797bf5.png)

The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0)+f(0.25)+f(0.5)+f(0.75)}})\cdot {{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $0$ | $0.25$ | $0.5$ | $0.75$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1+2+3+4)\cdot 0.25 \\  & =10\cdot 0.25 \\  & =2.5\end{aligned}
$$

Because the function is strictly $\text{increasing}$ over the interval $[0,1],$ the rectangles reach *below* the function, which means our approximation is an $\text{underestimate}$ of the actual area.
